catalog_quote: Keuw evidently has lexically contrastive tone. The wordlist contains a few (near-)minimal pairs, e.g., áalìyò ‘tongue’ versus áalíyò ‘house’; kíilyô ‘cuscus’ versus kíilíyò ‘arrow’; úukyò ‘grandfather’ versus úunyô ‘woman’. (Tonal diacritics follow IPA: acute indicates high, grave indicates low, circumflex indicates falling. Tone is marked only if it is known.) Many words begin with a sequence of high tones and shift to low or falling at some point. However, data is insufficient for an analysis of the tone system.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only description reports lexically contrastive tone (high, low, falling; at least two tones), with a recurrent word melody of initial high tones shifting to low/falling later in the word; the author explicitly says the data do not permit an analysis of the tone system. No claim of any kind is made about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None; tone left unmarked on words heard only in phrasal context; vowel length surface-variable and of unclear status.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical (word-level) tone in elicited citation forms from a 312-item wordlist; tones in the connected text were not transcribed. Silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Kamholz uses the name Keuw (SIL sources: Kehu); same language, kehu1238. Data from a few days of fieldwork (2008/2011) with two speakers from the single Keuw village on the Wapoga/Poronai area; Moxness 1998 second-hand wordlist reproduced as appendix.

Nothing at all is said about word stress (zero occurrences of 'stress'/'accent'). Abstract (p. 243): 'has at least two tones'.
Bibliographic check only: no grammar, sketch or phonology reference exists for Kehu; Kamholz 2012 is the sole descriptive work.
